title: The journeys of Jesus
method: Gospel-referenced itinerary, not a reconstructed GPS track. Chronological ordering blends the Gospel narratives and is debated, especially across John and the Synoptics. The slider shows narrative stops, not measured dates or distances. Each stop describes a recorded episode, not proof of a distinct trip. The first-pass evidence register documents corrected assumptions, unresolved scholarly issues and limited screening status at each stop. Each episode includes an original Scripture reading-context paragraph and canonical comparison references; this editorial depth must not be confused with independent academic verification.

sources.title: The canonical Gospels and Acts
sources.note: Primary references appear at each itinerary stop. Exact translations are opened in the licensed Scripture reader, not reproduced in this dataset.

sources.title: Historic biblical cartography
sources.note: Contextual comparison of regions and site uncertainty; not used as a definitive route.

phases.title: Birth and childhood
phases.description: From the birth narratives through Jesus at twelve

phases.title: Northern and eastern journeys
phases.description: Tyre, Sidon, Decapolis and Caesarea Philippi

phases.title: Journeys towards Jerusalem
phases.description: Feasts in Jerusalem and the final approach

places.name: Bethlehem
places.note: Birthplace; modern town location is well established.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Jerusalem is well identified. Specific Gospel buildings and first-century sites are not all archaeologically certain.

places.name: Egypt - unspecified refuge
places.note: Matthew names Egypt, not a town. This pin is a regional symbol, NOT a proposed residence or a known stopping point.

places.name: Nazareth
places.note: Childhood hometown; ancient settlement generally corresponds to modern Nazareth.

places.name: Jordan baptism area
places.note: Baptism is in the Jordan. The river point is illustrative; Bethany beyond the Jordan is disputed.

places.name: Wilderness - location unspecified
places.note: The Gospels name the wilderness, not its coordinates. This is an illustrative location only.

places.name: Bethany beyond the Jordan
places.note: John 1:28 and 10:40 describe a place beyond the Jordan. Candidate sites and its precise identification are debated.

places.name: Cana of Galilee
places.note: Traditional Kafr Kanna / archaeological Khirbet Qana identifications differ.

places.name: Capernaum
places.note: Ancient lakeside town at Tell Hum, a base for the Galilean ministry.

places.name: Judean countryside
places.note: John describes Jesus and his disciples in the Judean countryside without naming a town.

places.name: Sychar / Jacob's well
places.note: The Sychar identification is associated with the Jacob’s well site near modern Nablus; the precise settlement is debated.

places.name: Sea of Galilee shore
places.note: A regional map marker for lakeside teaching and journeys; it is not a specific landing point.

places.name: Galilean hillside
places.note: The Sermon on the Mount does not identify a particular hill. Traditional Mount of Beatitudes is not treated as proved.

places.name: Nain
places.note: Traditionally identified with modern Nein; exact ancient boundaries are not mapped.

places.name: Eastern Galilee shore
places.note: Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes vary among Gospel traditions/manuscripts. Marker suggests a district, not a proven town.

places.name: Bethsaida district
places.note: Bethsaida location debated between et-Tell, el-Araj and other proposed sites.

places.name: Gennesaret
places.note: The plain west of the lake is known; no exact arrival point is supplied.

places.name: Sidon / Sidon district
places.note: Mark describes travel through Sidon; it does not list visits to individual buildings.

places.name: Decapolis region
places.note: The Decapolis comprised cities and surrounding territory. This marker does not indicate a particular city.

places.name: Magadan / Dalmanutha region
places.note: The names in Matthew 15:39 and Mark 8:10 differ. Association with Magdala is debated.

places.name: Caesarea Philippi district
places.note: The district around Banias is named; not every conversation must have occurred inside the town.

places.name: High mountain - unspecified
places.note: The Transfiguration mountain is unnamed in the text. Both Tabor and Hermon have been proposed.

places.name: Samaritan village - unnamed
places.note: Luke 9:52-56 does not name the village. The pin represents Samaria generally.

places.name: Samaria-Galilee border
places.note: Luke 17:11 describes travel between regions without identifying a specific town.

places.name: Beyond the Jordan / Perea
places.note: The Gospels give a territory but no stop at this location; the pin is representative.

places.name: Bethany near Jerusalem
places.note: The town east of Jerusalem is usually associated with al-Eizariya.

places.name: Ephraim
places.note: John identifies a town called Ephraim; one proposed modern identification is et-Taiyibeh.

places.name: Jericho
places.note: Jericho is well attested but New Testament-era settlement encompassed a wider area than the modern town.

places.name: Bethphage
places.note: Gospel village near Mount of Olives, traditional location approximate.

places.name: Mount of Olives
places.note: The ridge east of Jerusalem is well known; exact speech/ascension positions are not established.

places.name: Gethsemane
places.note: Traditional garden location; ancient boundary and exact prayer spot unknown.

places.name: Emmaus - site disputed
places.note: Luke 24 names Emmaus, but multiple candidate sites exist; marker is illustrative, not a site identification.

places.name: Mountain in Galilee - unnamed
places.note: Matthew 28:16 gives no name for the mountain; marker represents Galilee as a region.

places.name: Tyre district
places.note: Jesus visited the region of Tyre; residence within the city is not specified.

places.name: Galilee - unspecified location
places.note: John reports travel into Galilee but does not identify a particular town at this point.

events.title: Birth of Jesus
events.summary: Jesus is born in Bethlehem during the census; the birth narratives identify Bethlehem in Judea.

study.context: Luke places the birth within a narrative about imperial registration and a journey to Bethlehem, while Matthew starts with Bethlehem in the days of Herod. Their accounts should be read in their own sequences; the census dating and precise modern year remain debated.

events.title: Presentation at the temple
events.summary: Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the temple; Simeon and Anna speak about him.

study.context: Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to the Jerusalem temple, where Simeon and Anna recognise his significance. Luke connects faithful worship, Israel's hope and an approaching sorrow; the scene does not independently establish the interval before Matthew's flight to Egypt.

events.title: Visit of the magi
events.summary: Magi visit the child and give gifts; Joseph is later warned of danger from Herod.
events.qualification: Matthew does not specify that the visit occurred on the night of the birth.

study.context: Matthew narrates visitors from the east following a star and paying homage to the child. Herod's inquiries and the visitors' changed return route matter more than a reconstructed travel map: Matthew gives neither their number nor an exact arrival day.

events.title: Flight into Egypt
events.summary: Joseph takes Mary and the child to Egypt after a warning in a dream, escaping Herod.
events.qualification: Matthew gives no Egyptian city, exact route, or length of residence.

study.context: Matthew describes Joseph leaving for Egypt after a warning and returning when danger passes. Egypt functions as refuge and is connected by Matthew to Hosea's language of God's son; no Egyptian city or route is supplied.

events.title: Return and upbringing in Nazareth
events.summary: The family settles in Nazareth; Jesus grows up there.
events.qualification: Matthew relates an Egyptian refuge before Nazareth; Luke moves from temple presentation to Nazareth without recording that episode. Their intervening sequence is not independently established.

study.context: Matthew associates the family's settling in Nazareth with the return from Egypt; Luke moves from Jerusalem temple duties to growth in Nazareth. The two narrative presentations cannot be merged into an independently timed itinerary by adding dates the texts do not give.

events.title: Passover pilgrimage at twelve
events.summary: Jesus remains at the temple among teachers while his parents search for him.

study.context: Luke's account of the twelve-year-old Jesus at Passover depicts sustained attention to discussion in the temple and parental concern. His return with his family frames the episode as childhood growth, not the start of a separately dated teaching tour.

events.title: Life in Nazareth
events.summary: Jesus returns to Nazareth with his parents and continues to grow.

study.context: Luke briefly describes Jesus' obedience to his parents and growth in wisdom, stature and favour. The summary gives an upbringing setting in Nazareth, rather than a dated sequence of travels or a record of every childhood event.

events.title: Baptism in the Jordan
events.summary: Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptised by John; the Spirit descends.
events.qualification: The exact bank/site is not settled by the text.

study.context: Jesus comes for baptism by John, and the Synoptic accounts connect the act to the Spirit and divine affirmation. Matthew, Mark and Luke describe the river setting, but the precise bank and present-day baptism-site claims need separate historical evidence.

events.title: Forty days and temptation
events.summary: Jesus fasts in the wilderness and answers the temptations with Scripture.
events.qualification: The wilderness is not a named mountain or precise site.

study.context: Matthew and Luke expand the temptation narrative with scriptural replies while Mark reports the wilderness period more briefly. The account speaks of testing and obedience rather than identifying a particular named peak, road or surveyed wilderness camp.

events.title: First disciples near John’s ministry
events.summary: John identifies Jesus, and two of John's disciples begin following him in this account.
events.qualification: The exact site of Bethany beyond the Jordan remains disputed; John's sequence relative to the Synoptics is reconstructed.

study.context: John's account presents the Baptist's testimony and disciples beginning to follow Jesus, including Andrew's introduction of Simon. 'Bethany beyond the Jordan' is the text's place designation, but its archaeological identification and chronology beside the Synoptic call narratives remain contested.

events.title: Journey into Galilee
events.summary: Jesus travels into Galilee and calls Philip, who speaks to Nathanael.
events.qualification: John 1:43 names Galilee, but not Nazareth or a specific stop on this journey.

study.context: In John, Jesus resolves to depart for Galilee and meets Philip, who then tells Nathanael about him. The narrative names the broader region and the disciples' responses but does not state an intermediate visit to Nazareth or specify a travel road.

events.title: Water turned into wine
events.summary: At a wedding in Cana, Jesus performs the first sign recorded by John.

study.context: John calls the Cana wedding sign the beginning of Jesus' signs, leading his disciples to believe. The social setting, abundance and sign language are central to John's purpose; an exact house or modern wedding venue cannot be proved from the story.

events.title: A brief stay after Cana
events.summary: Jesus stays in Capernaum with family and disciples for a few days.

study.context: John reports a short stay in Capernaum with Jesus' mother, brothers and disciples after the wedding. The few days mentioned form a bridge to Jerusalem, not a separate account of specific ministry acts in the town.

events.title: Passover and temple action
events.summary: Jesus goes to Jerusalem for Passover and drives merchants from the temple.
events.qualification: John places this temple action near an early Passover; Synoptics narrate a temple action in the final week. Whether one or two events are described is debated.

study.context: John places a temple confrontation near an early Passover and links it to the temple of Jesus' body. The Synoptics narrate a similar disruption in the last week; their relationship is a chronology question, not evidence for two independently dated actions.

events.title: Conversation with Nicodemus
events.summary: Jesus teaches Nicodemus about the new birth and entering the kingdom of God.
events.qualification: John 3 follows the Jerusalem setting; the conversation’s exact venue is not identified.

study.context: The night-time exchange with Nicodemus develops the themes of birth from above, the Spirit and believing in the Son. Jerusalem is inherited from John's surrounding setting, while the conversation itself supplies no identifiable building or street.

events.title: Ministry in Judean countryside
events.summary: Jesus and his disciples spend time in the countryside of Judea; the disciples baptise.
events.qualification: No town is named.

study.context: John describes Jesus and his disciples spending time in the Judean countryside and later discusses their baptising activity. The subject becomes how John's ministry relates to Jesus', while towns and precise Jordan approaches are not identified.

events.title: Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well
events.summary: Jesus speaks with a woman of Samaria and many people from the town come to believe.
events.qualification: Precise identification of Sychar is debated.

study.context: At Jacob's well, Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman about living water and worship, and the account expands to the town's response. John names Sychar and the well tradition, but the exact ancient settlement match and modern site's claim are separate questions.

events.title: Healing the official’s son
events.summary: Jesus returns to Cana and heals an official’s son, who is in Capernaum.
events.qualification: The son is in Capernaum, but Jesus is at Cana when he gives the word.

study.context: Jesus is at Cana when an official pleads for his son in Capernaum; the healing is described at a distance. Distinguishing the location of the speaker from the child's location prevents adding a Capernaum visit that the scene does not narrate.

events.title: Healing at Bethesda during a feast
events.summary: Jesus heals a man near the pool called Bethesda and teaches about his authority.
events.qualification: The feast is unnamed, so the visit's place in a harmonised chronology is uncertain.

study.context: John narrates a healing at a Jerusalem pool during an unnamed feast, followed by teaching about Jesus' authority and witness. The setting is identified in the narrative, but the unnamed festival does not secure this scene's date in a cross-Gospel harmony.

events.title: Teaching in the synagogue
events.summary: Jesus reads Isaiah in his hometown synagogue and faces rejection.
events.qualification: Luke presents the Nazareth synagogue appearance at a different narrative point from the hometown rejection in Mark 6 / Matthew 13; do not assume two proved visits or a secure unified order.

study.context: Luke places the Nazareth synagogue reading of Isaiah early and follows it with rejection. Mark and Matthew recount hometown rejection later; their sequence may reflect distinct presentations of an encounter rather than two proved visits.

events.title: Settling in Capernaum
events.summary: Jesus leaves Nazareth and lives in Capernaum on the shore of the lake.
events.qualification: Matthew 4:13 explicitly names Capernaum; the exact household or base of residence is not established.

study.context: Matthew reports Jesus leaving Nazareth for Capernaum and connects the Galilean setting with Isaiah's language about light. The town is named, but the account does not locate a specific household or establish every intermediate visit.

events.title: Calling the fishermen
events.summary: Jesus calls Simon, Andrew, James and John to follow him by the Sea of Galilee.
events.qualification: Matthew/Mark describe a lakeside call; Luke narrates the catch of fish in another presentation. Their precise relative sequence is not proved by these citations.

study.context: Matthew and Mark present a lakeside call of fishermen, while Luke presents a catch of fish and Simon's response. These are legitimate parallel readings, but their exact order and whether all details describe one meeting are interpretive matters.

events.title: Teaching and deliverance in synagogue
events.summary: Jesus teaches with authority and delivers a man from an unclean spirit.
events.qualification: Mark 1 places the fishermen's call before this synagogue scene, but Luke 4 narrates the Capernaum synagogue before the catch-and-call in Luke 5. The chronology comparison shows textual order, not separate independently dated events.

study.context: Mark narrates the call before Capernaum synagogue teaching, whereas Luke narrates the synagogue before the catch-and-call episode. The authority of Jesus' teaching is central; neither author supplies a modern calendar reconciling the accounts.

events.title: Healing in Simon’s household
events.summary: Jesus heals Simon's mother-in-law and later many sick and demon-oppressed people.

study.context: Simon’s mother-in-law is healed, followed by many brought to Jesus at evening. The house is presented as a place of hospitality and restoration, but neither Gospel names an excavated building as the verified scene.

events.title: Forgiving and healing a paralysed man
events.summary: Jesus pronounces forgiveness and heals a man lowered through a roof.
events.qualification: Mark 2:1 explicitly names Capernaum; the building itself is not securely located.

study.context: The paralysed man's friends overcome a crowd's obstruction to bring him before Jesus, who speaks of forgiveness and then heals. Mark places the event at Capernaum, while its roof and exact house cannot be matched to a surveyed structure.

events.title: Centurion’s servant healed
events.summary: Jesus responds to a centurion’s faith and the servant is healed.

study.context: The centurion's confidence in Jesus' authority prompts the servant's healing. Matthew describes direct dialogue and Luke reports intermediaries, so the two presentations should be compared rather than forced into one detailed reconstruction.

events.title: Teaching about the kingdom
events.summary: Jesus teaches on a mountain in Matthew and at a level place in Luke.
events.qualification: Do not equate the discourses or their locations with certainty.

study.context: Matthew's mountain teaching and Luke's level-place discourse overlap in ethics and kingdom themes but differ in framing and arrangement. The map groups them for study without claiming a single precisely located speech or an established shared date.

events.title: Widow’s son raised
events.summary: Jesus encounters a funeral procession at Nain and restores the widow’s son to life.

study.context: At Nain, Jesus encounters a widow during her son's funeral procession and raises him in Luke's account. The compassion and the town's response are explicit; a present-day procession route or house cannot be derived from the text.

events.title: Teaching beside the lake
events.summary: Jesus teaches crowds in parables from a boat.
events.qualification: Specific landing beach unnamed.

study.context: Mark describes teaching from a boat to a crowd gathered beside the lake, with parables interpreting different responses to the word. Matthew arranges a substantial collection of parables; neither supplies a precise shore location.

events.title: Storm calmed on the lake
events.summary: Jesus and the disciples cross the lake; Jesus stills wind and waves.
events.qualification: The travel line indicates movement across the lake, not the boat’s documented track.

study.context: The Synoptics relate a storm during a crossing and Jesus' command bringing calm. The contrast between fear and trust carries the narrative; the direction of the journey can be read from context, not the ship's surveyed course.

events.title: Deliverance on the eastern shore
events.summary: Jesus frees a demon-possessed man or men; the restored man proclaims what happened.
events.qualification: Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes are variant location traditions.

study.context: After the crossing, Jesus confronts demonic oppression in eastern lakeshore territory. Gospel manuscripts and traditions differ on Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes; this is regional narrative geography rather than a proven landing site.

events.title: Jairus’s daughter and the woman healed
events.summary: After Jesus crosses back to the lakeshore, a woman is healed and Jairus’s daughter is restored to life.
events.qualification: Mark 5:21 says Jesus is beside the sea after crossing; Capernaum is a plausible inference but is not named in the immediate episode.

study.context: On reaching the opposite shore, Jesus responds to a synagogue leader's plea while a woman is healed in the crowd. Mark names the lakeside but not Capernaum for the encounter, so a city-specific marker would overstate this passage.

events.title: A return to his hometown
events.summary: Jesus teaches again in his hometown, where people take offence at him.
events.qualification: Some harmonisations treat this as the same Nazareth rejection described by Luke.

study.context: Mark and Matthew describe neighbours taking offence when Jesus teaches in his hometown. Luke narrates a related confrontation earlier in his Gospel, so the second map entry denotes a textual presentation, not a confirmed extra return trip.

events.title: Feeding the five thousand
events.summary: Jesus feeds a crowd from five loaves and two fish near Bethsaida.
events.qualification: Luke associates this feeding with Bethsaida, while Mark and Matthew place it in a deserted setting. The exact site and the boat route are not fixed.

study.context: The five-loaves-and-two-fish feeding precedes a journey across the lake. Luke associates it with Bethsaida and other accounts stress a deserted place; neither supplies a definitive modern hillside or measured approach track.

events.title: Walking on the water
events.summary: During the night crossing, Jesus comes towards the disciples on the lake.
events.qualification: Mark 6:45 describes Bethsaida as the disciples' intended destination, but Mark 6:53 records their landing at Gennesaret; John 6:17 names Capernaum as a direction of travel. These accounts do not establish one surveyed route. The mapped crossing is schematic and does not identify a precise boat track.

study.context: Jesus comes to the disciples during their night crossing, and the accounts emphasise fear, recognition and rescue. Mark reports Bethsaida as an intended destination, Gennesaret as landfall, while John directs the travel towards Capernaum; none yields a measured course.

events.title: Healing in Gennesaret
events.summary: People recognise Jesus and bring the sick to him after the crossing.
events.qualification: Mark 6:53 explicitly reports landfall at Gennesaret. It follows Mark 6:45, which named Bethsaida as the intended destination; the difference should not be silently harmonised into a verified route.

study.context: Mark and Matthew record widespread healing after arrival in Gennesaret. The actual landfall named in Mark should be read against the preceding destination instruction toward Bethsaida, not silently conflated into one exact crossing.

events.title: Bread of life teaching
events.summary: Jesus teaches in the synagogue at Capernaum about the bread of life.

study.context: John locates the bread-of-life teaching in a Capernaum synagogue after the feeding and crossing. Themes of provision, faith and Jesus as the bread from heaven continue the narrative, while exact building archaeology is not part of this textual claim.

events.title: The Syrophoenician woman
events.summary: In the region of Tyre, Jesus responds to a mother asking for her daughter’s deliverance.
events.qualification: The text says region of Tyre, not a pinpoint house or street.

study.context: In the region of Tyre, Jesus responds to a Gentile mother's plea for her daughter. Mark and Matthew differ in presentation and terminology, and the region cannot be reduced to a proven house or single city point.

events.title: Journey by way of Sidon
events.summary: Jesus travels via Sidon towards the Sea of Galilee and Decapolis.
events.qualification: Mark reports a route via Sidon, not a distinct ministry episode inside the city.

study.context: Mark explicitly describes a journey through Sidon towards the Decapolis. This unusual circuit is a geographical narrative, but no independent healing or synagogue address in Sidon is reported at this stop.

events.title: A deaf man healed
events.summary: In the Decapolis region, Jesus opens a deaf man's ears and loosens his speech.
events.qualification: No specific town within the Decapolis is named.

study.context: Jesus heals a man who is deaf and has difficulty speaking in the Decapolis region. The scene focuses on his personal interaction and public reaction, without naming the town or a modern archaeological location.

events.title: Feeding the four thousand
events.summary: Jesus feeds a great crowd with seven loaves and small fish.
events.qualification: Exact site not named.

study.context: The second mass feeding is narrated with seven loaves and a large crowd, distinguished by Jesus' own later reference to the two feedings. Its location is a broad lakeside setting in Matthew, not a verified archaeological point.

events.title: Arrival in Magadan / Dalmanutha
events.summary: After the feeding, Jesus crosses by boat to a western lakeside district.
events.qualification: Magadan and Dalmanutha cannot be equated with complete certainty.

study.context: Matthew names Magadan and Mark names Dalmanutha after the feeding. The terms describe the arrival area differently and should be studied as parallel geographical witnesses, not assumed to prove that the two names are exact equivalents.

events.title: Healing a blind man
events.summary: Jesus takes a blind man outside Bethsaida, heals him and sends him home.

study.context: At Bethsaida, Jesus leads a blind man out of the village and restores his sight in stages. The village name is explicit in Mark, but the competing ancient-site identifications remain open questions and do not validate a particular modern house or road.

events.title: Peter’s confession
events.summary: In the Caesarea Philippi district, Peter declares Jesus to be the Christ.
events.qualification: Gospels identify the district, not a particular rock or shrine as the speech site.

study.context: Jesus asks his disciples who they say he is in the district of Caesarea Philippi, and Peter answers that he is the Christ. The region is specified in Mark and Matthew, but the scene is not placed at an identifiable rock, cave or shrine.

events.title: Jesus foretells his death
events.summary: After Peter’s confession, Jesus teaches about his coming suffering and the cost of discipleship.
events.qualification: The conversation follows the Caesarea Philippi setting without specifying a new stop.

study.context: Following Peter's confession, Jesus speaks openly of suffering, rejection, death and discipleship. The narrative carries on from the Caesarea Philippi district without supplying another named stop or a newly verified location.

events.title: The transfiguration
events.summary: Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James and John on an unnamed high mountain.
events.qualification: Mount Tabor and Mount Hermon are proposed traditions; the Gospel does not name the mountain.

study.context: The transfiguration narrative joins divine affirmation, Moses and Elijah, and the disciples' response to Jesus' glory. Matthew, Mark and Luke leave the mountain unnamed; identifying Mount Tabor or Hermon is a later geographical proposal.

events.title: Temple-tax discussion
events.summary: Jesus discusses the temple tax and the coin in the fish's mouth with Peter.

study.context: Matthew situates a discussion about the temple tax at Capernaum, ending with a coin from a fish to prevent offence. The town is named, but the narrative does not specify a particular house, fishing spot or tax-collection building.

events.title: Teaching about humility
events.summary: Jesus uses a child to teach his disciples about humility and welcome.

study.context: In Capernaum, Jesus places a child among the disciples to teach humility and welcome. Mark's account grows from their argument about greatness; Matthew organises related teaching in a wider discourse, so the exact framing varies.

events.title: A Samaritan village refuses welcome
events.summary: Jesus sends messengers to a Samaritan village that will not receive him.
events.qualification: Luke does not identify the village.

study.context: On the journey towards Jerusalem, a Samaritan village refuses hospitality because of the direction Jesus has set. Luke highlights his response to the disciples' proposed retaliation; the village is neither named nor locatable from the text.

events.title: Ten men with leprosy healed
events.summary: On the way towards Jerusalem, ten men are cleansed; one returns to give thanks.
events.qualification: Luke 17:11 describes travel at or between Samaria and Galilee, but its literary placement within the broader harmonised itinerary is not independently dated.

study.context: Luke narrates ten people with leprosy being cleansed while Jesus travels in the border country of Samaria and Galilee. The returning Samaritan's gratitude matters in the story; the verse does not define a single crossing point or precise date.

events.title: Feast of Booths teaching
events.summary: Jesus goes to Jerusalem for the festival and teaches in the temple.
events.qualification: John 7 and 8 contain feast-related teaching; John 7:53-8:11 is omitted from the earliest manuscripts as noted by the ESV, and is not silently included in this stop. The precise cross-Gospel ordering is unsettled.

study.context: At the Feast of Booths Jesus teaches publicly in Jerusalem and faces divided reactions. The passage register skips John 7:53-8:11, whose manuscript transmission is disputed; its omission here is deliberate rather than a claim of universal textual agreement.

events.title: Healing of a man born blind
events.summary: Jesus gives sight to a man born blind; authorities investigate the healing.

study.context: John describes Jesus healing a man blind from birth, followed by extended questioning and his witness. The scene is bound to Jerusalem and the pool of Siloam, but the social conflict and testimony are not reducible to an excavated coordinate.

events.title: Feast of Dedication
events.summary: Jesus teaches in Solomon’s Colonnade during the winter festival.

study.context: Jesus teaches during the winter Feast of Dedication in the temple's Solomon's Colonnade. John names this specific precinct and festival, but neither establishes the building's exact surviving footprint nor the event's date in a combined Gospel calendar.

events.title: Retreat across the Jordan
events.summary: Jesus goes again to the area where John had been baptising; many believe in him.
events.qualification: John does not give precise coordinates.

study.context: John says Jesus returned beyond the Jordan to the area where John had first baptised. This establishes a relationship with earlier Baptist testimony, but does not yield an undisputed modern Bethany-beyond-the-Jordan site.

events.title: Lazarus raised
events.summary: Jesus comes to Bethany and calls Lazarus from the tomb.

study.context: In Bethany, Jesus speaks with Martha and Mary amid grief and calls Lazarus from the tomb. John gives a named village near Jerusalem, while identifying an exact surviving tomb or dating a particular visit requires different evidence.

events.title: Withdrawal to Ephraim
events.summary: Jesus withdraws to a town called Ephraim near the wilderness.
events.qualification: The site identification is debated.

study.context: After opposition grows, John says Jesus withdraws to Ephraim near the wilderness with his disciples. The town's identity and modern site remain debated, so the stop is a narrative place-name rather than a certified location.

events.title: Ministry beyond the Jordan
events.summary: Jesus teaches and heals in the territory across the Jordan.
events.qualification: Region only; cannot assert a particular Perea town.

study.context: Matthew and Mark place ministry in the region across the Jordan following earlier Galilean activity. The general geographical designation is not a list of named Perea towns, and it cannot establish a precise border crossing.

events.title: Blind man healed near Jericho
events.summary: A blind beggar receives sight as Jesus approaches or leaves Jericho.
events.qualification: Luke 18:35 presents the healing as Jesus approaches Jericho; Mark 10:46 and Matthew 20:29 describe departure from Jericho. Matthew mentions two blind men, while Mark names Bartimaeus. These accounts are grouped for comparison, not proof of a single precise roadside location or an undisputed itinerary.

study.context: Mark and Matthew describe a healing as Jesus leaves Jericho, while Luke places a related account on the approach and Matthew names two men. These differences should remain visible when reading accounts together; no exact roadside point is established.

events.title: Zacchaeus welcomed
events.summary: Jesus calls Zacchaeus from a tree and stays with him.

study.context: Luke describes Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, receiving Jesus and responding with restitution and generosity. The named Jericho setting is explicit, but the particular sycamore tree or host dwelling cannot be identified by the passage.

events.title: Dinner in Bethany before Passover
events.summary: A meal is held for Jesus; Mary anoints his feet in John’s account.
events.qualification: The relationship to the anointing account in Mark 14 and Matthew 26 is debated.

study.context: John places a dinner in Bethany before Passover and describes Mary anointing Jesus' feet. Mark and Matthew recount an anointing at Bethany in a different narrative position; the entries are parallel texts, not proof of two separate meals.

events.title: The donkey is brought
events.summary: Near Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, disciples bring a colt for the journey into Jerusalem.
events.qualification: The Gospels place the approach near Bethphage and Bethany; the village where the donkey was obtained is not securely identified as Bethphage.

study.context: The disciples obtain a colt as Jesus approaches Jerusalem near Bethphage and Bethany. The accounts describe instructions involving a village, but do not independently identify that village with Bethphage or fix its modern position.

events.title: Approach from the Mount of Olives
events.summary: Jesus comes down the Mount of Olives as the crowd rejoices, and he laments over Jerusalem.

study.context: Luke recounts the crowd's praise as Jesus comes down from the Mount of Olives, followed by his lament over Jerusalem. The landscape is broadly identified, but the scene supplies no exact overlook or road coordinate.

events.title: Entry into Jerusalem
events.summary: Crowds welcome Jesus as he enters the city.

study.context: All four Gospels narrate Jesus entering Jerusalem to acclamation, but their choice of details and emphasis varies. The procession's meaning is described in Scripture; a single reconstructed urban route is not given in the narratives.

events.title: Temple action in the final week
events.summary: Jesus challenges buying and selling in the temple precinct.
events.qualification: Relationship to the earlier temple action in John 2 is disputed.

study.context: In the final week the Synoptic accounts describe Jesus challenging commerce in the temple precincts. John's earlier temple action is a disputed parallel, so the map should not use these separate literary positions as proof of two distinct episodes.

events.title: Evenings in Bethany
events.summary: Jesus goes outside the city to Bethany during the final week.

study.context: Mark and Matthew note Jesus leaving Jerusalem for Bethany during the final days. These brief travel notices establish a recurring village setting without identifying a particular lodging house on every evening.

events.title: Debates and teaching in the temple
events.summary: Jesus teaches about authority, resurrection, the great commandment and warnings against hypocrisy.

study.context: The temple debates bring together questions of Jesus' authority, resurrection, Scripture and the greatest commandment. The Synoptics organise the material differently, so this grouped entry is a teaching sequence, not one uninterrupted speech.

events.title: Teaching on the Mount of Olives
events.summary: Jesus speaks of the temple and coming events while seated opposite it.

study.context: Jesus' teaching on the Mount of Olives follows the disciples' questions about the temple and coming events. Matthew, Mark and Luke preserve different emphases; identifying every prediction with a single securely dated later event requires interpretation.

events.title: Anointing in Simon’s house
events.summary: At Bethany, a woman anoints Jesus in Simon the leper’s house in the Synoptic accounts.
events.qualification: Matthew and Mark locate an anointing at Bethany but introduce it later in their narrative than John 12. Whether the accounts describe the same meal or separate occasions is debated. Do not count them as two proved visits.

study.context: Mark and Matthew place an anointing at Simon the leper's house in Bethany. John records a related meal involving Mary; the similarities and differences invite comparison but do not prove a second event or additional journey.

events.title: Last Supper
events.summary: Jesus shares a final meal with the disciples; Synoptics describe bread and cup, while John records foot-washing and farewell teaching.
events.qualification: Synoptics describe Passover preparation and meal; John introduces supper before Passover. The chronology/calendar and precise room are debated; this map does not resolve them.

study.context: The Synoptics present preparations for Passover and bread-and-cup teaching, while John frames supper before Passover and emphasises foot-washing and farewell teaching. Their relationship to Passover dates is debated; the venue and calendar are not mapped as certainties.

events.title: Prayer and arrest
events.summary: Jesus prays in Gethsemane and is arrested after Judas arrives.
events.qualification: Location of the traditional garden is approximate.

study.context: The Gospels describe prayer, distress, Judas' arrival and arrest after the supper. Synoptic accounts name Gethsemane, while John's account identifies a garden across the Kidron; the traditional modern garden's exact boundaries are not independently proved.

events.title: Hearings before authorities
events.summary: Jesus is questioned before religious and Roman authorities and sentenced.
events.qualification: Exact routes between hearing venues are not established.

study.context: Jesus is brought before Jewish and Roman authorities in the passion narratives. The Gospels differ in the order and selection of hearings; grouping them for study does not establish a precise route between identifiable surviving buildings.

events.title: Crucifixion at Golgotha
events.summary: Jesus is crucified outside the city; the Gospels record his death and burial preparations.
events.qualification: Golgotha is named, but the precise physical site remains debated.

study.context: The Gospels identify Golgotha as the place of crucifixion and report Jesus' death in distinct narrative presentations. A named site within ancient Jerusalem need not imply that every later commemorative location is archaeologically certain.

events.title: Burial in a tomb
events.summary: Joseph of Arimathea places Jesus in a tomb before the Sabbath.
events.qualification: The location of the tomb is represented by Jerusalem, not a verified surveyed point.

study.context: Joseph of Arimathea secures Jesus' body and places it in a tomb ahead of the Sabbath. The texts supply burial context and witnesses, not the surveyed coordinates of a tomb proven beyond competing historical proposals.

events.title: The empty tomb and appearances
events.summary: The Gospels report the empty tomb and appearances of the risen Jesus.
events.qualification: Accounts differ in the presentation of visitors and sequence; no single modern site is assumed.

study.context: The empty-tomb accounts describe visitors, a missing body and messages of resurrection, with differences in order and emphasis across the four Gospels. Mark 16:1-8 is cited deliberately; the longer ending at 16:9-20 has a documented manuscript history and is not silently treated as undisputed.

events.title: Appearance on the road to Emmaus
events.summary: The risen Jesus walks with two disciples, explains the Scriptures and is recognised at a meal.
events.qualification: Several competing locations for Emmaus; the marker is illustrative.

study.context: Luke tells of two travellers who recognise the risen Jesus at a meal after he interprets the Scriptures. Emmaus is named and a distance indicated, but its geographical identification remains disputed and the map does not resolve all proposed sites.

events.title: Appearances to the gathered disciples
events.summary: The Gospels describe appearances to gathered disciples; John also records a later meeting involving Thomas.
events.qualification: John 20:19-29 narrates an appearance and another eight days later involving Thomas. Luke 24 also reports an appearance. This stop groups accounts, not one single evening.

study.context: Luke and John report appearances to gathered disciples, and John distinguishes a later encounter when Thomas is present. This event groups related accounts without claiming that all episodes occurred in one continuous evening.

events.title: Appearance by the Sea of Tiberias
events.summary: Jesus appears by the lake, directs a catch of fish and speaks with Peter.
events.qualification: The shoreline location is unspecified.

study.context: John describes Jesus appearing beside the Sea of Tiberias, directing a catch of fish and questioning Peter about love and pastoral care. The scene is located on the lake generally, not at an authenticated modern shoreline point.

events.title: Commission on a mountain in Galilee
events.summary: The risen Jesus meets the eleven and sends them to make disciples of the nations.
events.qualification: The mountain is unnamed, and Matthew does not establish its timing relative to John 21. The chosen order is editorial.

study.context: Matthew places the commission to the eleven on a mountain in Galilee. Its identity is unnamed and its timing relative to John's lakeshore appearance is not specified; the map's sequence is an editorial reading order.

events.title: Ascension near Bethany
events.summary: Jesus blesses the disciples near Bethany; Acts associates the return with the Mount of Olives.
events.qualification: Luke 24:50 describes Jesus leading the disciples toward Bethany; Acts 1:12 places their return from the Mount of Olives. These identify a broad area, not surveyed coordinates for the ascension, and do not supply a continuous dated route for all resurrection appearances.

study.context: Luke places Jesus' blessing and departure towards Bethany, while Acts refers to the disciples returning from the Mount of Olives and later describes the time since resurrection. These texts locate a broad area, not a pinpoint site; textual variants in Luke 24:51-52 need their own manuscript-critical consideration.

contextCoverage.scope: All 79 Gospel journey entries include distinct original biblical reading-context notes and canonical comparison passages. Existing chronology, location and first-pass issues remain; this is not a comprehensive independent historical or textual audit.
contextCoverage.method: AI-assisted source-first narrative context and parallel-passage comparison across the Gospel itinerary. Source links address particular text-critical, chronological and site interpretations; unpublished underlying routes are not inferred.
contextCoverage.limitations: Canonical texts are primary sources for their respective narrative and doctrinal claims, not archaeological proof of event locations. Further publisher-accessible source examination, original-manuscript work, independent historical review and flagship navigation QA remain v1.0 tasks.
